structure_read: §1 Introduction (motivation: corner count grows; SSTA alternatives; proposed flow; states the approach targets non-final STA runs)
§2 Background: §2.1 slack equations for setup (Eq. 2) and hold (Eq. 4); §2.2 corner dominance, endpoint coverage, dominant set, dominance margin, with a 4-endpoint/4-corner example

§3 Experimental setup: 15 industrial 45nm circuits, 5 reported (T1-T5, 916K-1,419K instances); 15 corners = 3 device settings x 5 interconnect settings; setup/hold derates (+/-5%); CRPR applied; top-25% worst-slack endpoints analyzed; Table 5 clock periods 4, 3.9, 2.2, 3, 1 ns
§4 Arrival-time dominance: c14/c15 dominate maximum arrivals, c1/c2 dominate minimums

§5 Slack dominance: §5.1 setup coverage of the slow set CM={c14,c15} (Table 8) at margins 0/10/20/30 ps; §5.2 hold coverage varies per circuit across candidate sets Cm, Cb, Cw (no small fixed set suffices)

§6 Hold method: §6.1 anchor corner full run plus partial (clock-network-only) runs and the skew-change estimate (Eqs. 6, 8, 9, 10) with error term (Eq. 11); §6.2 accuracy (Table 11), SI effects (Table 12), conservatism (Table 13), runtime (Table 14)
findings_supported: F-2 (setup-coverage, hold-estimate, partial-run cost and benchmark-composition observations)
key_observations: Setup result is an empirical coverage measurement with a dominance margin, presented as a reasoned expectation, not a proof or a certificate: worst-case setup slacks are 'expected to occur' at the corners with the largest arrivals (§5.1), and coverage of the two slow corners is 99.9% at a 30 ps margin, 97.9% at 10 ps, with the weakest circuit at 87.6% at 0 ps (Table 8).

Hold: the estimate replaces the true slack change by the clock-skew change between the anchor corner and a partial (clock-network-only) corner (Eqs. 8-10); the remaining error is the datapath-delay change plus the required-hold-time change (Eq. 11); usefulness requires e_d > 0; no exact refinement or fallback is described and the multi-startpoint remedy is dismissed (§6.1).

Reported accuracy of the hold estimate: coverage 'very close to' the full set with over 98.6% for T2/T4/T5 at a 5 ps margin (Table 11); with SI, above 98.4% for T1-T4 but 92.1% for T5 (Table 12); conservatism means about -1 to -2 ps with worst cases about -26 to -38 ps, described as 'can be conservative by up to -40ps' (§6.2.3, Table 13).

Runtime: partial runs 9.0-25.3 s against full runs 490.9-2466.6 s; speedups 2.4x-3.6x including per-run overhead, over 4.1x (up to 4.7x) when overhead is shared (Table 14). The clock-only partial run is therefore roughly 1-5% of a full run per corner on this industrial 45nm setup.

The paper makes no exactness or guarantee claim anywhere: 'guaranteed' appears only negatively (any set guaranteed to bound hold slacks must include a large number of corners); 'exact' appears only to say that capturing the exact worst case, or knowing the exact slack change, would require full runs; the method is stated to target non-final STA runs, with additional corners added at sign-off.

Corners vary interconnect (RC and C) as well as device settings: 3 device x 5 interconnect settings. Device settings are best/typical/worst with temperature inversion excluded but described as extendable.
limitations: Industrial 45nm circuits and an unnamed commercial flow; not reproducible on the packet's open toolchain.

The extraction route introduces a fidelity risk for quoted wording; section-level structure and numbers were consistent across four independent question passes, but this is not the same as reading the PDF myself.
Results are restricted to the top-25% worst-slack endpoints and to flop-to-flop paths (ports excluded), so coverage percentages are not statements about all endpoints of the designs.
Copyright: only bounded fragments are stored; the full text is not copied into this outbox.

records.title: A Linear-Time Approach for Static Timing Analysis Covering All Process Corners (Onaissi, Najm)
records.source_type: paper (author-hosted PDF of the IEEE TCAD 2008 journal version)
records.retrieved: 2026-10-13 (UTC session window; read through the extraction proxy route of C-A02)
records.access_caveat: Same proxy-extraction fidelity caveat as C-A01: section-level content and claims are reliable at that granularity; exact wording remains for the verifier to confirm.
key_observations: Delay, arrival time and slew are modelled as affine linear functions of normalized process parameters in [-1, +1]; each parameter takes the value -1 or +1, so the parameter space reduces to 2^n discrete corners and the maximum is sought only at corners. Combinational circuits and setup-type constraints are the focus.
The internal max operation is proven conservative by construction (a hyperplane ceiling over its inputs; the paper states it never wants to underestimate maximum delay or slew at any process corner).

End-to-end, however, the result is an approximation, not a rigorous bound: the linearized interconnect delay, slew and effective-capacitance inputs 'are not conservative and might underestimate values at certain corners'. This is stated by the authors as a known limitation.

Accuracy is empirical (ISCAS '85 benchmarks, 90nm library), with a reported runtime speedup of roughly six to seven times over corner analysis and O(mn) complexity against the corner approach's exponential dependence on n.

No slack formulation, and no exact refinement or per-corner fallback: the minimum-overestimation hyperplane would need an exponential-complexity linear program and is rejected in favour of a linear-time heuristic; accuracy is verified afterwards against exhaustive corner runs.
Hold is stated to be applicable as is, but the paper develops setup (maximum delay and slew) and shows minimum delay and slew charts; per-corner slack decisions are not its object.
limitations: Benchmarks are ISCAS '85 with a 90nm library; no industrial designs.
A soundness claim about the internal max operator does not transfer to the reported delay values, which the paper itself says can be underestimated at some corners.
Read through the extraction proxy; the two-sentence non-conservatism statement is the load-bearing quote and should be confirmed by the verifier.

records.title: Design for Variability and Signoff Tips (A. Tetelbaum, Abelite Design Automation)
records.source_type: vendor white paper (same author and host as the proposer's SRC-019)
key_observations: Judging a corner 'redundant or dominated' from a single sub-path's max or min is unsafe: minimum slack combines launch, data and capture sub-path delays, and the paper names the concrete pattern SS + Fast-Metal as required for setup when launch and data paths are cell-delay dominated while the capture path is metal-delay dominated; the mirror pattern FF + Vmax + Slow-Metal is also named. It warns of 'risk of missing violations in paths with rare bad structures'.

Delay is not monotone in temperature: 'sub-path delay is not a monotonic function of T' (temperature inversion), and extreme delays may occur at any temperature, so it recommends more than two or three temperature corners at final signoff.

Compensation practice for reduced corner counts: start with increased OCV/AOCV derates to find potential violators, then re-run those violators with regular derates to filter false ones; use sufficiently large margins.
No formal guarantee is claimed for corner removal; the paper states the corner-based approach 'does not guarantee against a silicon failure'.
limitations: Vendor white paper promoting the author's statistical signoff methods; it supports statements about practice and failure modes, not controlled measurements.
Predates the pilot by a decade; used for the qualitative structure of the failure mode and the absence-of-guarantee statement.

records.title: MMMC corner pruning: dominance pruning under the PVT x mode combinatorial explosion, and missed-signoff risk control (translated title), 极客工场
records.source_type: secondary explainer article (Chinese-language site, no named author)
key_observations: Defines scenario A dominating B when no path is better at A than at B, so that B's violations are subsumed by A and B can be pruned from the setup signoff list.

Gives three levels of evidence: (1) library delay monotonicity — a scripted scan of Liberty delay tables showing corner A at least as slow as B for every cell, described as the strongest and cheapest test and treated as a mathematical proof at the cell level; (2) RC-pairing monotonicity, a comparability condition between library and parasitic corners; (3) path-structure sampling, explicitly not a proof but engineering confidence, requiring recorded sample size.
States that temperature inversion and multi-voltage domains push corners into the non-provable third tier.

Reports a representative mid-size SoC scenario list shrinking about 5:1 (roughly 320 to 60) and recommends auditable per-pruned-scenario records, automatic re-expansion when a backbone corner shows near-zero slack (|slack| under 30 ps), and a protected golden full-corner re-run before tapeout.
limitations: Secondary source with no named author; per docs/EVIDENCE.md it can guide discovery but cannot decide novelty or soundness.

Its claim that cell-level monotonicity is a proof is about the cell level only; C-A07 shows why cell-level dominance does not automatically give slack-level dominance. The article does not resolve that gap.
Used only as a lead that dominant-corner pruning is practitioner knowledge; a primary source must be found before any objection relies on it.

records.source_type: citation index query
records.access: metadata (titles, years, venues and abstracts of 23 citing works)
key_observations: 23 citing works were returned. By title and abstract, they fall into: learned or statistical cross-corner prediction (One-for-All ICCAD 2024; FACT MLCAD 2024; Unobserved Corner DATE 2019; multi-corner timing macro modeling TCAD 2024; SI-aware wire timing prediction ASP-DAC 2025; several earlier ML OCV works); parallelism (CPU-GPU heterogeneous STA, TCAD 2023); mode merging (A timing graph based approach to mode merging, DAC 2015); library characterization (SetupKit ICCAD 2025); hold fixing and clock-skew work; and unrelated sensors/SoC papers.

No citing work, at title/abstract level, presents sound per-scenario certification with exact refinement against characterized-table semantics; the dominant theme is prediction without guarantees, which is consistent with the proposer's statement of the gap.

Shortlist that still deserves a full-text check: 'NIO: A fast and accurate verification method for PVT variations' (2014), 'A timing graph based approach to mode merging' (DAC 2015), and 'Circuit performance verification and optimization in the presence of variability' (2011).
limitations: Abstract-level only; cannot decide novelty. The proposer could not run this query (Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 during their session); it ran for me, so the proposer's forward-citation gap is now partially closed by a different session.
The API list is not guaranteed complete.

records.title: The TAU 2018 Contest (Timing Contest on Path Reporting), presentation deck
records.source_type: workshop contest deck (primary: the contest organizers' own slides)
key_observations: Contest topic: 'Timing Contest on Path Reporting' - report generation over a pre-built timing graph, with from/through/to query support; graph-based analysis only.

Benchmarks: TAU 2015 designs vga_lcd (139.5K gates) and leon3mp_iccad (1247.7K gates); about 50K paths per testcase pre-generated by a commercial timer; special constant-delay Liberty models were used 'to reduce delay-calculation impact'.
Scoring: accuracy 30%, runtime 30%, memory 20%, documentation 20%.
No multi-corner/multi-scenario problem: corners appear only as 'Early and Late Libraries' supplied as inputs. Nothing asks for scenario coverage, corner reduction or a guarantee across PVT.
Resolves part of the proposer's U8 (CLM-014 'TAU 2018 and 2019 topics unresolved').
limitations: Deck, not a paper; contest scope statements are authoritative but terse.

records.title: TAU 2019 Contest: A Parallel Closure (Design Optimization Contest), presentation deck
records.source_type: workshop contest deck (primary: the contest organizers' own slides)
key_observations: Contest topic: 'Design Optimization Contest' - an optimizer applying buffer insertion/deletion and buffer re-sizing, evaluated by a timer (OpenTimer); the stated goals are to explore incrementality and parallelism of optimizations inside static timers.

Benchmarks based on TAU 2015: s1196 (641), systemcdes (3441), usb_funct (15743), vga_lcd (139529), leon2_iccad (795371), leon3mp_iccad (659017) gates; Nangate FreePDK45 Generic Open Cell Library with area and power information; several designs are flagged '(no spef)'.
Inputs include 'Early and Late Libraries' and SPEF; result tables are split into fast-corner and typical-corner columns.
Scoring: Performance (max clock frequency) 100, Power 50, Area 50, Runtime 70, Memory 30, Documentation 100 (400 total).

No part of the contest problem asks for multi-corner scenario coverage, reduction, screening or a soundness guarantee across PVT; the multi-library structure is an input-format feature (early/late for min-max analysis), not a scenario-reduction objective.

Resolves the rest of U8. Side-product: this benchmark package is a candidate source of multi-library, multi-design data (6 designs, Nangate45, SPEF) for the pilot's dataset gap (CLM-013), subject to licence and to the caveat that early/late libraries are not separate PVT scenarios.
limitations: Deck only; no corner count per benchmark; whether 'fast' and 'typical' are two characterized PVT corners or two analysis views is not stated and must not be assumed.

records.title: The Elmore Delay as a Bound for RC Trees with Generalized Input Signals (Gupta, Krauter, Tutuianu, Willis, Pileggi), DAC 1995
records.source_type: paper (UC Irvine DAC compendium archive; the proposer's SRC-026, previously metadata only)
records.access: full (direct extraction; the PDF's text streams are LZW-compressed, handled by this session's extractor)
verified_quotes: Abstract: 'we prove that the Elmore delay is an absolute upper bound on the 50% delay of an RC tree response. Moreover, we prove that this bound holds for input signals other than steps, and that the actual delay asymptotically approaches the Elmore delay as the input signal rise time increases. A lower bound on the delay is also developed using the Elmore delay and the second moment of the impulse response.'

COROLLARY 2: 'For an RC circuit with a monotonically increasing, piecewise-smooth input u(t) such that u'(t) is a unimodal symmetric function, [delay <= TD] holds for the output response y(t) at any node.'

COROLLARY 3: 'For a finite sized RC circuit with a monotonically increasing, piecewise-smooth input u(t) with rise-time tr, such that u'(t) is a unimodal symmetric function, as tr -> infinity, TD -> 50% delay.'

Section IV: 'It has been shown above that the Elmore delay is an upper bound on the 50% step response delay. However, when using the Elmore delay to estimate RC interconnect delays, the signal from a digital gate is generally modeled by a saturated ramp.'

Author-stated limitations: uncertainty whether the metric is optimistic or pessimistic, and the restriction to step-response delay estimation; accuracy improves with distance from the driving point and with rise time (Table 2: node A 104% error at tr=1ns, 1.54% at 10ns).

Theorem conditions are stated for RC trees (tree structure is used in the induction proofs); networks with floating capacitors or resistor loops are not covered by any stated theorem; Corollary 3 adds the 'finite sized RC circuit' qualifier.
consequences: The cited source supports an upper bound on the 50% delay of the TRUE RC tree response under stated waveform conditions. The pinned calculator returns a different quantity: the crossing time of a pi-model waveform model (measured from the driver source waveform's own crossing) at driver thresholds, then possibly adjusted by thresholdAdjust (C-A16). P4 needs an argument connecting the two; the theorem alone does not supply it.
This record closes the proposer's SRC-026 metadata-only status.
limitations: Extraction is from a compressed-text PDF; formulas are readable only as scrambled runs. Quoted statements are prose, cross-checked at multiple occurrences.

records.title: CRPR sign in the pinned OpenSTA: clock reconvergence pessimism REDUCES hold slack (basis for OBJ-001)
records.source_type: source code (pinned commit; hash-verified tree, see C-A13)
locators: search/PathEnd.cc lines 691-710 (verbatim): commonClkPessimism returns '-crpr_' when checkRole's generic role is hold, '+crpr_' otherwise; requiredTime = requiredTimeNoCrpr + commonClkPessimism.
search/PathEnd.cc lines 1015-1020: PathEndCheck::clkSkew subtracts crpr_ and subtracts target clock uncertainty, with the comment 'Uncertainty decreases slack, but increases skew'.
sdc/Sdc.cc lines 226-229: constructor sets analysis_type_ = AnalysisType::ocv and crpr_enabled_ = true (crpr_mode_ = CrprMode::same_pin).
sdc/Sdc.cc lines 5474-5477: Sdc::crprActive() returns analysis_type_ == AnalysisType::ocv && crpr_enabled_.
tcl/Variables.tcl lines 50-70: set_crpr_enabled and crpr_mode are the user-visible controls.
key_observations: With the pinned defaults (OCV analysis type, crpr enabled), the reference engine applies CRPR to every constrained path end: setup slack increases by crpr, hold slack decreases by crpr.
Therefore 'give no credit in the bound ... CRPR only adds slack' is conservative for setup and UNSOUND for hold: an omitted -crpr term makes the hold bound too large.
The exact clock pass (pass A of the proposal's mechanism) already computes both clock paths at the check, so crpr is available to the certificate without extra delay calculation.
limitations: Static code reading; no execution. Whether the pilot's flows leave the defaults untouched is a flow question (EXP-001), not a code question.

records.title: thresholdAdjust in the pinned OpenSTA: the reported wire delay can be raised above the single-pole crossing when driver and load libraries differ (basis for OBJ-002)
records.source_type: source code (pinned commit; hash-verified tree, see C-A13)
locators: dcalc/DelayCalcBase.cc lines 126-153: thresholdAdjust applies only when the load pin's library differs from the driver's library; for a rise it adds load_slew * (load_vth - drvr_vth)/(drvr_slew_upper - drvr_slew_lower) to the delay and subtracts the same for a fall; it also rescales the slew by the ratio of slew windows/derates.
dcalc/DelayCalcBase.cc lines 155-169: thresholdLibrary uses the default (first-read) Liberty library for top-level ports.
dcalc/DmpCeff.cc lines 569-570: comment stating the load delay/slew are measured at driver thresholds and rely on thresholdAdjust to convert to the load's thresholds.
dcalc/DmpDelayCalc.cc lines 96, 121, 276, 343 and dcalc/LumpedCapDelayCalc.cc line 162: thresholdAdjust applied to the wire delay after the calculator returns it.

dcalc/DelayCalcBase.cc lines 107-124: dspfWireDelaySlew (input-port DSPF path) computes wire_delay = -elmore * log(1 - vth) with a load slew from the exponential model - a distinct wire-delay formula for top-level ports.
key_observations: CLM-007's description ('single-pole crossing with tau = Elmore delay, with Elmore fallbacks') describes the DmpAlg/DmpPi path but omits two code realities: (1) the value returned to the timing engine can be a threshold-adjusted one that is LARGER for rise arcs when load_vth > drvr_vth; (2) top-level ports are served by a different wire-delay formula (dspfWireDelaySlew, delay = -elmore*ln(1-vth), which for vth=0.5 is 0.694*elmore).
Both realities bear on P4, whose upper bound is 'the Elmore delay of the reduced model'.
limitations: Static code reading; the magnitude of the adjustment depends on library thresholds and on whether a scenario reads more than one Liberty library (or on port arcs).

records.title: Machine-Learning-Based Multi-Corner Timing Prediction for Faster Timing Closure (MDPI Electronics 11(10):1571, 12 May 2022; NUDT Changsha)
records.url: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/11/10/1571 (read through the extraction proxy route of C-A02)
records.source_type: journal paper, gold open access
records.access_caveat: Read through the third-party extraction proxy; section-level content is reliable, exact wording is not guaranteed. A direct byte fetch of the publisher mirror (res.mdpi.com path guess) returned an empty body and was recorded as a failed route.
records.proposer_previous_access: abstract-level (SRC-022 was grouped with SRC-023 to SRC-025 as prediction literature)
key_observations: Method: a learned multi-corner slack predictor built on a 'dominant corner selection strategy' (the paper's 'iterative increase strategy'). Exact STA is run on the selected dominant corners; a Random Forest model (compared with Ridge and MLP) predicts slack at the remaining corners; a performance assessment form exposes speed-versus-accuracy trade-offs.
No formal guarantee and no uncertainty-triggered fallback to exact analysis: the industrial flow 'used the model to replace the STA tool on 12 corners', with 2 dominant corners timed exactly.

Signoff-safety language is a practical-equivalence claim, not a proof: MAE below 3 ps 'can be regarded as having the same effect as the STA tool in practical industrial applications', justified by an observation that predicted results are useful when the error is under 10 ps. The paper does not address undetected violations from a mispredicted corner.

Hold-centric data: 14 hold corners at a 16nm process; designs are ITC'99 b17/b18/b19 plus in-house cache/peripheral/CPU blocks (ind1 512KB 16-way L2, ind2 out-of-order superscalar); clock periods 2 ns and 0.43 ns.

Relevance to the candidate: this is the nearest accessed work that sells 'replace the tool on most corners' for HOLD, with no certificate and no refinement. It strengthens CLM-002/L1 at full-text level and is a natural H3 (safety-contrast) comparator; it also shows dominant-corner selection being applied to hold, which bears on F-4's dominance-pruning discussion.
limitations: Proxy route (C-A02 caveat).
Author names were not recoverable from the extracted text (contributions list initials only); the affiliation (NUDT) and title are confirmed.
Not decisive for novelty either way; it is a prediction method, not a screening certificate.

records.title: US 12,675,622 B1 'Signoff-safe multi-corner reduction for static timing analysis' (Synopsys) — claim-level read
records.source_type: granted patent, primary text
records.access: full (claims, description, bibliographic data read live)
records.proposer_previous_access: SRC-017 was in the proposer's source set; this read establishes exactly what the claims cover and what the 'signoff-safe' language is attached to
key_observations: Independent claim 1 (method): select a first set of paths; compute slack and component-feature values across a first set of corners; store a path library; pick a dominant corner (the one worst for the most paths); compute slacks for a second path set at the dominant corner; estimate slacks at non-dominant corners by feature matching within a tolerance; choose a second set of corners for each path; mark circuit objects with those corners. Claims 8 (CRM) and 15 (apparatus; second path set larger than the first) mirror claim 1.

Dependent claim 7: two ML models — a first model decides whether an error in a predicted slack is below a threshold; a second predicts the slack. Claims 3/4: an 'aggressiveness level' controls how many corners are kept; claim 5: selection via a cost function.

The signoff-safety sentence is in the Description, not the claims: 'Embodiments described herein are designed to be sign-off safe in that if no violations are reported by the embodiments, then no violations exist across all corners that are being considered.'

TNS is explicitly approximate in the Description: the aggressiveness 'may be set to a level that maintains a consistent TNS error percentage' (worked example: a 1% TNS difference vs. full timing). Nothing in the claims or embodiments requires exact violation lists, exact TNS, or exact refinement of the candidate corner set; results are hedged as 'acceptable differences in quality of results'.

Bibliographic: assignee Synopsys; inventors Clerkin, Sripada, Ghanta, Tehrani, Li; priority 2022-04-25 (provisional 63/334,566); filed 2023-04-18; granted 2026-07-07; examiner-cited prior art includes Synopsys US8701063B1, 'Compressing scenarios of electronic circuits'.
limitations: Claim construction is a legal question; the read above reports what the text says, not a validity or freedom-to-operate opinion.

records.source_type: journal/conference records, abstract-level (API reads) and summary-level (search index) as marked
records.access: abstract-level: ASAP (S2 API), FACT (Crossref API), One-for-All (S2 API), multicorner TCAD 2024 (S2 API), flip-flop TODAES 2025 (S2 API). Summary-level: SetupKit (ICCAD 2025), BLAST (DAC 2025), SI-Aware (ASP-DAC 2025), uncertainty-aware GNN (IEEE 11566436).

FACT, MLCAD 2024 / TODAES 31(4), 2026 (DOI 10.1145/3768166; online 2025-09-15): full-corner metrics from timing analysis 'under only one known corner' via correlations across technology files, targeting near-threshold nonlinearity; no guarantee language in the abstract.

One-for-All, ICCAD 2024 (DOI 10.1145/3676536.3676656): one known corner predicts all unknown corners; 'average accuracy enhancement of 62.6% and 95.3%' on two processes, MAE under 0.37 ps / 0.01 ps, over 10x ECO speedup; empirical only.

Multicorner Timing Analysis Acceleration, TCAD 43(7):2151-2162, 2024: Bayesian decision strategy 'to deliver reliable predictions with accuracy close to 100%', improving 'prediction accuracy to 100% with little extra STA executions' — a statistical fallback, not a certificate; no exactness claim.

SetupKit, ICCAD 2025: multi-corner setup/hold characterization with bias-enhanced interpolation and active learning; 2.4x CPU reduction on industrial 22nm cells across 16 PVT corners — a library-characterization problem, adjacent rather than competing.
SI-Aware Wire Timing Prediction at Pre-Routing Stage with Multi-Corner Consideration, ASP-DAC 2025: appears as a 2025 citing work of SRC-012; not read (citation only).

BLAST, DAC 2025 late-breaking: bisection-free statistical timing characterization; relative RMSE 2.21% and worst-case absolute error 0.82 ps across 135 PVT corners (TSMC 12nm) — the rare explicit worst-case *error metric*, still a measurement, not a guarantee.

Machine Learning-Driven Flip-Flop Timing Model, TODAES 2025 (DOI 10.1145/3785294): ML latch-probability model plus a second C2Q model, applied to 'hierarchical violation filtering' (reported 100% precision on their data); a waiver/filtering application with measured, not proven, safety.

Towards Robust Pre-Routing Timing Prediction: An Uncertainty-Aware GNN (IEEE 11566436): heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL for prediction variance, aimed at avoiding 'silent failures' out of distribution; uncertainty quantification, no hard bound.
limitations: Mixed fidelity: five entries are API abstract reads, four are search-index summaries; no 2025-2026 closed-access item was obtained at full text. The K1 judgment in F-12 is made at this fidelity and should be re-checked if any full text becomes available.

records.title: TAU industry deck read: Synopsys 'Clustering-based signal merging in STA' (Belov, Wrixon, Keller, Dadheech; presented TAU 2019, hosted on the 2020 site) — merge-only-when-converged framing with explicit accuracy control
records.source_type: workshop slide deck, primary industry source
key_observations: Subject is the GBA-PBA accuracy gap: GBA (graph-based, BFS) is linear-cost but pessimistic; PBA is exact per path but exponential; merging signals in PBA is how tools recover runtime.

The deck's safety framing is explicit: 'No convergence => no merging => slacks are accurate' — merging is only applied where convergence holds, and the partition is chosen to 'minimize overall accuracy [loss]' at a given merge factor.
Industrial data point: 16nm block at 0.545V, 100K endpoints; 40% of endpoints have a GBA-PBA gap below 0.05 ns.

Relation to the candidate: this is industry practice on merging with an accuracy criterion, adjacent to (but different from) corner reduction and screening; it closes the F-13 lead and can serve as a practitioner reference if the proposal's related work discusses reduction practice.
limitations: Slide-level text; no formal statement of the convergence criterion in the extracted text.

NIO: A fast and accurate verification method for PVT variations (ICSICT 2014; DOI 10.1109/ICSICT.2014.7021608): IEEE-paywalled; Semantic Scholar holds the title with no abstract; no open copy found. Remains unread — recorded as unobtainable within this session's routes rather than silently dropped.

Onaissi PhD thesis (U Toronto, 2011; same author as SRC-012/013): Ch. 4 is a block-based PSTA 'covering all potentially critical paths' with a section 'Exact Algorithm' (4.4.1) and a 'Sufficient Condition' (4.4.2); Ch. 5 is the DAC 2011 anchor-corner method with a section 'Exact vs conservative approach' (5.2) and conservatism statistics. Conservatism is conditional: 'for our technique to be conservative we must choose, for each set of corners, an anchor corner that leads to the smallest datapath delay'. In the optimization chapter the no-guarantee statement is explicit: 'there is no guarantee that X-hat would be the worst-case corner for the post-optimization expression'. CRPR appears in the margin discussion as a pessimism-removal technique.

Net effect: the thesis strengthens F-1/F-5 at a fuller-text level — the SARI line is anchor-based and conditionally conservative with empirical characterization, has an exact *parametric PSTA* algorithm as a separate chapter (a different object from engine-exact screening), and contains no per-scenario certificate with exact refinement.

arXiv/OA negative result: properly formed arXiv API queries (title-field and AND-combined) returned zero preprints for ASAP (TCAD 2026), SetupKit (ICCAD 2025), BLAST (DAC 2025), the uncertainty-aware GNN, and SI-Aware (ASP-DAC 2025); One-for-All's ACM 'open access' PDF link returns HTTP 403 from this session. No open full text of the five closed 2025-26 works exists at the routes available, so F-12's fidelity caveat is now a verified negative rather than an untried check.
limitations: Thesis text extraction drops some ligatures (fi/ff) and can break words across lines; keyword contexts were read with whitespace normalization, and quoted fragments above are short.

records.title: ASAP7 multi-VT libraries share identical threshold attributes: mixed-VT alone does not trigger thresholdAdjust (OBJ-002 condition narrowed)
records.source_type: PDK library files, primary (streamed through grep; files not retained)
records.access: attribute-level (headers inspected for threshold and nominal attributes)
key_observations: All three ASAP7 stdcell variants (LVT, RVT, SLVT) declare identical timing-threshold attributes: input_threshold_pct_fall/rise 50, output_threshold_pct_fall/rise 50, slew_lower 10, slew_upper 90, and identical nom_voltage 0.7 / nom_temperature 25 / default_operating_conditions PVT_0P7V_25C.

Consequence for OBJ-002: with load_vth == drvr_vth the additive thresholdAdjust term is zero, so reading several VT-flavored libraries in one corner (the normal pattern, e.g. ISPD 2026's libworst) does not by itself move the returned wire delay. The live condition is narrower: a library pair whose threshold pct attributes *differ* (some macro/IO libraries use different definitions), or the separate input-port formula (dspfWireDelaySlew).
This narrows my own objection's 'potentially major' branch; the CLM-007 completeness point and the P4 modelling obligation are unaffected.
limitations: Three library headers checked (AO family); other ASAP7 families (OA, INVBUF) assumed identical, not verified. Files were not retained, so no hash is recorded; the check is reproducible from the URL pattern.
